evidence_registry.speaker: Jillian
evidence_registry.text: How many women did you study?

evidence_registry.speaker: Jillian
evidence_registry.text: Do patients mind not having as many doctor's appointments? Because, I mean, there's, I know, I've been pregnant four times. The thought is, is that, you worry every time, right?

evidence_registry.speaker: Jillian
evidence_registry.text: Yeah. You actually look forward to going to the doctor, and yes.

evidence_registry.speaker: Jillian
evidence_registry.text: I would think personally, if a doctor were to say to me, “listen, I’m going to give you this kit, now I'm not going to, I'm only going to see you half of the time, this will take care of the rest of it,” I would have a problem with that, actually.

evidence_registry.speaker: Jillian
evidence_registry.text: How many women did you study?

evidence_registry.speaker: Jillian
evidence_registry.text: But how can you generate that much data just from a scale and a cuff? Isn't that just the weight and the blood pressure?

evidence_registry.speaker: Jillian
evidence_registry.text: And listens to the baby, you listen to the baby's heart.

evidence_registry.speaker: Jillian
evidence_registry.text: I mean, there's a lot of things. You know, I'm a little concerned that it's not just the blood pressure, and it's not just the weight.

evidence_registry.speaker: Jillian
evidence_registry.text: But just so you know, that would have been, I mean a doctor's visit would have found that out as well.

evidence_registry.speaker: Jillian
evidence_registry.text: Why can't the woman just have a cuff and step on the scale and put it into the app? I mean, and just communicate it with the doctor that way? This is my, have a little piece, a little calendar in the app, and every day she just goes in, tells what her weight is, tells what her blood pressure is once a week, and you're good to go.

evidence_registry.speaker: Jillian
evidence_registry.text: Well there's no data. You take your weight, you take your blood pressure, done.

evidence_registry.speaker: Jillian
evidence_registry.text: So what does that represent in terms of patients?

evidence_registry.speaker: Jillian
evidence_registry.text: In the last...? Because you've launched over the last year.

evidence_registry.speaker: Jillian
evidence_registry.text: You're raising $3.5 million and the valuation is what?

evidence_registry.speaker: Jillian
evidence_registry.text: I, um, I love this. For so many reasons. I'm personally and professionally connected to this. So what I'd like to do is I'd like to do $500,000.

evidence_registry.speaker: Jillian
evidence_registry.text: And what I'd like to do with that is — and just to be clear, I have a venture fund which is Structure Capital, and I have my own. So I would like to bring this to them to either do all of the $500,000, or to break this out so that I do a piece of this, they do a piece of this, and then our LPs, who get to directly invest, have the opportunity to do this. But I'd like you to carve out $500,000 for us.

rationales.explanation: Queries the breadth of the study evidence involving women using the product.
Characterizes the study population as limited to only 50 women.
Queries whether patients find fewer prenatal appointments acceptable and reassuring.
States that patients look forward to in-person doctor visits, indicating reduced visits may diminish appeal or reassurance.
Directly states that replacing half of the doctor visits with the kit would be personally unacceptable.
Again queries the size of the study supporting patient use of the product.
Reiterates that the evidence base consists of only 50 women.
Questions whether the product can credibly generate substantially more data than basic weight and blood-pressure measurements.
Points out that in-person prenatal care includes listening to the baby's heart, an omitted product function.
Expresses concern that prenatal care involves more than blood pressure and weight.
States that a normal doctor's visit would also have detected the cited condition, weakening the product's distinctiveness.
Questions whether a simpler self-reporting workflow could provide the same core functionality.
Rejects the claimed additional data value by reducing the workflow to taking weight and blood pressure.
Queries the number of patients represented by the company's health-system presence.
Queries the time period behind reported revenue to assess the maturity of traction.
Queries valuation alongside the financing amount, enabling assessment of valuation relative to company progress.
Directly expresses strong positive reaction to the company and uses that reaction immediately before stating the investment amount.
States that she is personally and professionally connected to the opportunity, directly linking personal alignment to her investment interest.

unmapped_utterances: [7] This is Jillian Manus, my fund is Structure Capital.
[8] You can have the most incredible product, but if you don’t know how to talk about it, you’re going to have a problem accelerating it.
[90] So what are you raising? And what are the terms?
annotation_summary: Jillian's observed In decision is explicitly supported by her positive reaction and personal/professional connection to Babyscripts, followed by a $500,000 commitment and requested carve-out. Earlier utterances primarily question patient acceptance, product completeness, differentiation, study scope, adoption, traction timing, and valuation.
